blocks.content: Five philosophers, five forks, one simple rule. This tiny setup manages to pack deadlock, starvation, and mutual exclusion into a single, unforgettable problem.

Five philosophers sit around a circular table. Between each adjacent pair sits exactly one fork, so there are five forks total. To eat, a philosopher must pick up BOTH the fork to their left and the fork to their right, then put both down when finished.

Each fork represents a shared resource that only one philosopher, neighbor, can use at a time. This is exactly the kind of contention real systems face constantly with limited shared resources, like database connections or file locks.

Suppose every philosopher simultaneously picks up their LEFT fork first. Now every single fork is held by exactly one philosopher, and every philosopher is stuck waiting forever for their right fork, which their neighbor is holding.

blocks.content: Number the forks, and require every philosopher to always pick up the LOWER numbered fork first, regardless of which side it happens to be on. This forces the highest numbered philosopher to reach for their forks in the opposite order from everyone else.
That single asymmetry is enough to guarantee the circular chain can never fully close, since at least one philosopher is always waiting in the other direction.

Only allow at most 4 of the 5 philosophers to attempt picking up forks at the same time. With one philosopher always sitting out, there is guaranteed to be at least one fork free at any moment, so someone can always complete their pair.
A philosopher must ask a central arbitrator, a waiter, for permission before picking up any forks. The arbitrator only grants permission in a way that never allows a deadlock cycle to form.
8. Why This Is Such a Popular Teaching Tool
blocks.text: 8. Why This Is Such a Popular Teaching Tool

blocks.content: The problem is small enough to state in a single paragraph, yet rich enough that solving it correctly requires understanding deadlock conditions AND at least one real concurrency control technique. That combination is rare and valuable in a teaching example.

["Proposing \"just pick up both forks atomically\" without describing a concrete mechanism for how that atomicity is actually achieved.","Forgetting that a correct solution must avoid BOTH deadlock and starvation, not deadlock alone."]
items: Proposing "just pick up both forks atomically" without describing a concrete mechanism for how that atomicity is actually achieved.
Forgetting that a correct solution must avoid BOTH deadlock and starvation, not deadlock alone.

blocks.content: This problem is a fitting close to the Synchronization and Concurrency module. It touches race conditions, mutual exclusion, semaphores or monitors as the implementation tool, and deadlock, all in one small, memorable scenario.
